gloss: To call on a law, a right, or an authority as a reason or a source of support.
examples: Witnesses can *invoke* the Fifth Amendment and say nothing.
The governor *invoked* emergency powers the night of the flood.
The same clause has been *invoked* three times this year.
contrast: You *invoke* a rule or a power, but you *evoke* a memory or a feeling.

gloss: To have something as a necessary part or a necessary result.
examples: Does the job *involve* much travel?
The repair *involved* pulling out the whole engine.
It is a long process, *involving* three separate forms.

transitivity: both — transitive (*X-rays ionize the air*), intransitive (*the gas ionizes at high temperatures*)
gloss: To give atoms or molecules an electric charge by adding or removing electrons.
examples: Strong radiation can *ionize* the air inside the chamber.
The gas *ionized* the moment the voltage rose.
Hospitals limit how much *ionizing* radiation a patient receives.
contrast: American spelling is *ionize*; British writing uses *ionise*.

gloss: To expose something to radiation, usually to kill germs or to treat a disease.
examples: Some countries *irradiate* imported fruit to kill insects.
The tumor was *irradiated* over six weeks.
The plant is *irradiating* spices around the clock.

gloss: To list things one by one, especially the separate costs on a bill.
examples: Please *itemize* every expense on the form.
The mechanic *itemized* the parts and the labor.
We asked for an *itemized* receipt at checkout.
contrast: American spelling is *itemize*; British writing uses *itemise*.

ru: дорабатывать версию за версией, повторять цикл
transitivity: both — transitive (*they iterate the design weekly*), intransitive (*good teams iterate fast*)
gloss: To repeat a process, improving the result a little each time.
examples: Small studios *iterate* instead of waiting for a perfect plan.
We *iterated* on the layout until it finally felt right.
They have been *iterating* on the same screen all month.
contrast: *Iterate* means to repeat and improve; *reiterate* means to say something again.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he jabbered something about a delay*), intransitive (*they jabbered all the way home*)
gloss: To talk fast and at length in a way that is hard to follow.
examples: The twins *jabber* at each other from morning to night.
He *jabbered* something about a missed connection and ran off.
She fell asleep with the radio *jabbering* in the corner.

ru: складываться пополам (о фуре с прицепом), сложиться
gloss: For a truck and its trailer to fold sharply toward each other and go out of control.
examples: Empty trailers *jackknife* easily on black ice.
A semi *jackknifed* across two lanes of the interstate.
Traffic stopped behind a *jackknifed* tanker.
contrast: The noun makes the plural *jackknives*, but the verb takes a plain *-s*: *it jackknifes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he jangled his keys*), intransitive (*her bracelets jangled*)
gloss: To make a harsh ringing noise, the way loose metal does.
examples: Loose change *jangles* in his coat pocket.
The keys *jangled* as the guard walked past the cell.
Three cups of coffee left her nerves *jangling*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the pothole jarred my back*), intransitive (*the color jars with the rest of the room*)
gloss: To give something a sudden unpleasant shake or shock.
examples: Sirens *jar* him awake almost every night.
The hard landing *jarred* every passenger forward.
It was a *jarring* end to a very quiet evening.
contrast: The consonant doubles: *jar → jarred, jarring*.

gloss: To cross a street illegally, away from a crosswalk or against the light.
examples: People *jaywalk* all over midtown at lunchtime.
She *jaywalked* to catch the bus before it pulled away.
He got a forty-dollar ticket for *jaywalking*.

gloss: To come together into something that finally works, such as a team, a plan, or an idea.
examples: Give the group a month and they will *jell*.
The offense finally *jelled* in the second half.
Her argument was still *jelling* when the deadline hit.
contrast: Also written *gel* in American English; both spellings sound the same.

ru: ставить под угрозу, подвергать опасности; поставить под угрозу
gloss: To put something valuable at risk of being lost or damaged.
examples: One careless email could *jeopardize* the whole deal.
The delay *jeopardized* their visa applications.
Funding has been *jeopardized* by the audit.
contrast: American spelling is *jeopardize*; British writing uses *jeopardise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*she jerked the rope*), intransitive (*the train jerked forward*)
gloss: To move, or to move something, with one short sudden pull.
examples: Never *jerk* the wheel on an icy road.
He *jerked* his hand back from the hot pan.
The elevator started *jerking* between floors.

gloss: To throw away or abandon something you no longer want or can no longer carry.
examples: Pilots *jettison* fuel before an emergency landing.
The party *jettisoned* the proposal as soon as the polls came out.
Half the schedule was *jettisoned* to save money.

gloss: To agree with something else or fit together with it.
examples: These numbers do not *jibe* with last quarter's report.
His account *jibed* with what the neighbors told police.
The two timelines were not *jibing*, so we checked again.
contrast: *Jibe* takes *with*, and it is a different word from *gibe* (to mock) and *jive* (music, or nonsense talk).

transitivity: both — transitive (*jiggle the key*), intransitive (*the mirror jiggles*)
gloss: To move, or make something move, with quick short shakes.
examples: *Jiggle* the key a little and the lock opens.
He *jiggled* the handle until the toilet stopped running.
The dashboard was *jiggling* the whole way down the gravel road.

gloss: To suddenly end a romance with someone you were expected to marry.
examples: Nobody expects a groom to *jilt* the bride an hour before the ceremony.
She *jilted* him by text message.
The *jilted* fiancé kept the ring and the deposit.

gloss: To force a lock, door, or window open with a bar or a tool.
examples: A thief can *jimmy* that window in about ten seconds.
Someone *jimmied* the back door and took two laptops.
He was caught *jimmying* the latch with a screwdriver.
contrast: The *-y* becomes *-ie* before *-s* and *-d* (*jimmies*, *jimmied*) but stays in *jimmying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he jingled the coins*), intransitive (*the bells jingle*)
gloss: To make a light ringing sound, like small bells or loose coins.
examples: Coins *jingle* in the donation box by the door.
The dog's tags *jingled* all the way down the hallway.
He walked in *jingling* a set of car keys.

gloss: To bring bad luck to someone or something, often by mentioning it too soon.
examples: Do not *jinx* it — there are still two innings left.
I said the word shutout and *jinxed* the whole game.
This car feels *jinxed*.
contrast: The third person adds *-es*: *he jinxes it every time*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he jockeyed the truck into the loading bay*), intransitive (*six candidates jockey for the same seat*)
gloss: To maneuver for advantage, especially by pushing past rivals.
examples: Six candidates *jockey* for the same endorsement every spring.
The two firms *jockeyed* for the contract all year.
Reporters were *jockeying* for a spot near the podium.
contrast: A vowel comes before the *-y*, so it stays: *jockeyed*, not *jockied*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*she journals her dreams*), intransitive (*he journals every morning*)
gloss: To write regularly in a personal diary about your thoughts and your days.
examples: She *journals* for ten minutes before work.
I *journaled* through the whole move.
*Journaling* helped him think the decision through.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *journaled*, *journaling*; British writing doubles it.

gloss: To travel, especially over a long distance.
examples: Thousands *journey* to the coast every summer.
The family *journeyed* west by wagon in 1847.
He spent two years *journeying* through South America.
contrast: The *-ey* stays: *journeyed*, never *journied*.

gloss: To fight on horseback with lances, or, in a figurative sense, to spar with someone in argument.
examples: Knights *joust* at the fair every July.
The two senators *jousted* for an hour on live television.
He enjoys *jousting* with reporters after a game.

gloss: To squeeze the liquid out of fruit or vegetables, or informally to boost something.
examples: *Juice* two lemons for the dressing.
The rebate was meant to *juice* holiday spending.
She has been *juicing* carrots and beets every morning.

gloss: To mix things together so that they end up in no order at all.
examples: Do not *jumble* the receipts — I sorted them by month.
The move *jumbled* everything in the garage.
Her notes were *jumbled* together in one folder.

ru: дать толчок, запустить; завести от другого аккумулятора
gloss: To get something moving quickly, or to start a car using cables from another battery.
examples: A tax rebate could *jumpstart* consumer spending.
A neighbor *jumpstarted* my car in the parking lot.
They are *jumpstarting* the project with outside money.
contrast: Often written with a hyphen: *jump-start*.

gloss: To throw something away as worthless, or to drop a plan entirely.
examples: We should *junk* the old printer and buy a new one.
The city *junked* the plan after the hearing.
Two hundred buses were *junked* last year.

gloss: To stick out past a surface or an edge.
examples: Sharp rocks *jut* from the water at low tide.
A nail *jutted* up through the board.
The balcony, *jutting* out over the street, blocked all the light.
contrast: The consonant doubles: *jut → jutted, jutting*.

gloss: To put two things side by side so that the difference between them shows.
examples: Good editors *juxtapose* the two photographs on purpose.
The film *juxtaposed* wealth and poverty on the same block.
*Juxtaposing* the drafts shows how much he cut.

gloss: To make something begin or become active in a hurry.
examples: A small grant can *kickstart* a business.
That one interview *kickstarted* her career.
The city is *kickstarting* the season with a free concert.
contrast: Often written with a hyphen: *kick-start*.

gloss: To hit someone with your knee.
examples: The coach warned them never to *knee* an opponent.
She *kneed* him in the thigh going for the rebound.
He was *kneed* twice before the referee stepped in.
contrast: The *k* is silent, and the past *kneed* sounds exactly like *need*.

gloss: To stab or cut someone with a knife.
examples: Two men tried to *knife* him outside the bar.
Someone *knifed* the tires on every car in the lot.
He was *knifed* in the arm during the robbery.
contrast: The noun makes the plural *knives*, but the verb takes a plain *-s*: *he knifes*.

ru: посвящать в рыцари, посвятить в рыцари
gloss: To give someone the rank of knight in a formal ceremony.
examples: British monarchs *knight* actors, athletes and scientists.
The queen *knighted* him in 1965.
She was *knighted* for her work in medicine.
contrast: The *k* is silent: *knight* sounds exactly like *night*.

gloss: To behave in an excessively obedient way toward someone powerful.
examples: She refuses to *kowtow* to the board.
The paper *kowtowed* to its advertisers for years.
Critics accused the mayor of *kowtowing* to developers.
contrast: Both syllables rhyme with *now*, not with *know*, and the verb takes *to*.

gloss: To work hard at something slow and difficult.
examples: Crews *labor* through the night after every storm.
He *labored* over that speech for a week.
The old engine was *laboring* on the last hill.
contrast: American spelling is *labor*, *labored*; British writing uses *labour*, *laboured*.

gloss: To cut or tear skin deeply and roughly.
examples: Broken glass can *lacerate* a hand in an instant.
The fall *lacerated* his knee.
She came in with a *lacerated* scalp.

gloss: To coat wood or metal with a hard glossy varnish.
examples: They *lacquer* each box by hand.
He sanded and *lacquered* the tabletop over the weekend.
A *lacquered* red tray sat by the register.

gloss: To serve liquid food with a large deep spoon.
examples: *Ladle* the soup into warm bowls.
Volunteers *ladled* stew for four hundred people.
She stood at the pot, *ladling* chili onto rice.

gloss: To criticize someone or something harshly and in public.
examples: Columnists *lambaste* the plan every other week.
The coach *lambasted* his defense after the loss.
She was *lambasted* online for one careless remark.
contrast: Also spelled *lambast*; either way the stress falls on the second syllable.

transitivity: both — transitive (*they lament the loss of the theater*), intransitive (*the whole town gathered to lament*)
gloss: To express deep sorrow or regret about something.
examples: Older residents *lament* the loss of the corner store.
He *lamented* that nobody reads the local paper anymore.
Critics have long *lamented* the state of the building.

gloss: To cover something with a thin protective layer, or to build it up out of thin layers.
examples: They *laminate* every ID card at the front desk.
I *laminated* the recipe so it would survive the kitchen.
The counter is *laminated* to look like marble.
contrast: The verb ends LAM-uh-nayt; the noun and adjective end LAM-uh-nuht.

gloss: To mock someone publicly with humor, especially in writing or a sketch.
examples: Late-night shows *lampoon* every candidate in turn.
The cartoon *lampooned* the mayor's new haircut.
He has been *lampooned* on television for twenty years.

gloss: To be left somewhere in a bad or forgotten state for a long time.
examples: Bills can *languish* in committee for years.
The proposal *languished* on someone's desk all summer.
Thousands of cases are still *languishing* in the courts.

transitivity: both — transitive (*latch the gate*), intransitive (*the door will not latch*)
gloss: To fasten something with a small bar or catch.
examples: Please *latch* the gate behind you.
He *latched* the screen door and turned off the porch light.
The window has not been *latching* properly since the storm.
contrast: The third person adds *-es*: *it latches*.

gloss: To praise someone or something highly, usually in public.
examples: Critics *laud* the film for its honesty.
The mayor *lauded* the firefighters by name.
She has been widely *lauded* for the research.
contrast: *Laud* (LAWD, to praise) is not *loud* (LOWD).

gloss: To make the sounds and the face that show you find something funny.
examples: Babies *laugh* before they can talk.
Everyone *laughed* when the microphone squealed.
She was *laughing* so hard she had to sit down.
contrast: The *gh* is pronounced /f/: LAF, and the past is LAFT.

gloss: To give something very generously, even excessively, to someone.
examples: Grandparents *lavish* attention on the youngest child.
The company *lavished* bonuses on its sales team.
He has been *lavishing* gifts on her since June.
contrast: The verb takes *on*: *lavish praise on someone*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*rain leaches nutrients out of the soil*), intransitive (*chemicals leached into the creek*)
gloss: To drain away through soil or another material, or to wash something away that way.
examples: Heavy rain *leaches* nitrogen out of the topsoil.
Lead *leached* into the drinking water for months.
Old pipes are still *leaching* metal into the supply.
contrast: *Leach* sounds exactly like *leech*, the blood-sucking worm.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the phone leapfrogged its rivals*), intransitive (*the kids leapfrog across the lawn*)
gloss: To jump ahead of others, skipping the usual steps in between.
examples: Cheap solar let some countries *leapfrog* the power grid entirely.
She *leapfrogged* two colleagues to become director.
The company is *leapfrogging* a whole generation of hardware.
contrast: The *g* doubles: *leapfrogged*, *leapfrogging*.

gloss: To look at someone in an unpleasant, openly sexual way.
examples: Men at the back table *leer* at every waitress.
He *leered* at her across the bar.
She caught him *leering* and moved seats.
contrast: The verb takes *at*: *leer at someone*.

gloss: To make something seem lawful, acceptable, or respectable.
examples: Coverage like that can *legitimize* fringe ideas.
The election *legitimized* the new government.
Critics say the award is *legitimizing* very bad science.
contrast: American spelling is *legitimize*; British writing uses *legitimise*.

gloss: To use something you already have in order to gain a further advantage.
examples: Small firms *leverage* social media to reach customers.
She *leveraged* her contacts into a much better job.
They are *leveraging* the brand to sell insurance.

ru: левитировать, парить в воздухе; поднимать в воздух
transitivity: both — transitive (*the magician levitated his assistant*), intransitive (*the table seemed to levitate*)
gloss: To rise and float in the air with no visible support.
examples: Magicians appear to *levitate* a foot above the stage.
He *levitated* a coin above his open palm.
Dust hung in the beam of light, *levitating* there for a minute.

gloss: To make laws, rules, or an economy less strict and more open.
examples: Several states plan to *liberalize* their liquor laws.
The country *liberalized* trade in the 1990s.
Banking has been steadily *liberalized* since then.
contrast: American spelling is *liberalize*; British writing uses *liberalise*.

gloss: To say that one thing is similar to another.
examples: Coaches often *liken* a season to a marathon.
She *likened* the debate to a food fight.
His style has been *likened* to early Hemingway.
contrast: The verb always takes *to*: *liken one thing to another*.

gloss: To be alive, or to have your home in a particular place.
examples: Both my sisters *live* in Chicago.
He *lived* alone in that house for thirty years.
They have been *living* out of suitcases since May.
contrast: The verb is LIV, rhyming with *give*; the adjective in *a live broadcast* is LYV.

ru: локализовать, определять местоположение; адаптировать под рынок
gloss: To limit something to one area, or to adapt a product for a particular country.
examples: Doctors could not *localize* the source of the pain.
The studio *localized* the game for eleven markets.
The outbreak has been *localized* to two counties.
contrast: American spelling is *localize*; British writing uses *localise*.

gloss: To stand or wait around in a place with no clear purpose.
examples: Signs ask people not to *loiter* near the entrance.
Teenagers *loitered* outside the theater until midnight.
He was stopped for *loitering* in the parking garage.

gloss: To turn your eyes toward something, or to seem a certain way.
examples: *Look* both ways before you cross.
She *looked* tired the whole week.
He was *looking* straight at the camera.
contrast: *Look* is about directing your eyes; *see* is about what your eyes take in, and *watch* is about following something over time.

gloss: To sit or lie in a relaxed, lazy way.
examples: On Sundays they *lounge* by the pool all afternoon.
He *lounged* on the couch with the game on.
Guests were *lounging* in the shade when we arrived.
